newsitem.title: USA: Shuttle crew rest after undocking from Mir.
newsitem.headline: Shuttle crew rest after undocking from Mir.

text.p: As the crew of the U.S. shuttle Atlantis relaxed on Tuesday after separating from Russia's Mir space station, NASA officials studied a new problem with one of the rocket launch boosters.

Atlantis pulled away from the orbiting outpost at 9:33 p.m. EDT on Monday (0133 GMT Tuesday) after five days of joint operations. The six shuttle astronauts, including the returning Shannon Lucid, took four hours off work on Tuesday.
"It was a well deserved break for the crew as they wind down their activities and prepare to head home," said NASA spokeswoman Pam Alloway.

Atlantis is scheduled to return to Earth on Thursday. Touchdown is planned at 8:12 a.m. EDT (1212 GMT) at Florida's Kennedy Space Centre, but weather conditions could force a diversion to Edwards Air Force Base in California.
NASA tightened the landing weather rules because of the unexpected failure of one of Atlantis' three hydraulic power units shortly after the shuttle entered orbit.
Space agency officials said on Tuesday they were studying unusual damage to one of the twin solid rocket boosters used to launch Atlantis on Sept. 16.

A post-flight inspection revealed a series of troughs burned into the protective insulation that lines the nozzle of the right-hand booster. The deepest troughs cut up to a half-inch (1.25 cm) into the material, which varies from 1.5 to 3 inches (3.75-7.5 cm) in thickness.

NASA officials, who have been particularly sensitive to booster problems since the 1986 Challenger explosion, said they had seen similar damage on at least five earlier shuttle flights, but never to the same extent.
The two 149-ft (45-metre) long boosters provide most of the shuttle's liftoff thrust until they peel away two minutes into flight. The rockets are later retrieved from the Atlantic Ocean for reuse.
The boosters replaced an earlier set thought to contain flaws in their joint seals.
Engineers considered the problem minor but an inquiry was underway to determine its cause, said NASA spokeswoman June Malone.
"We understand the power that goes with these solid rocket motors," she said. "So anytime we see something new or different we try to understand what's happening."

The shuttle Atlantis left Mir after picking up Lucid and dropping off her replacement John Blaha. About 6,000 lbs (2,700 kg) of cargo was transferred to and from the station while the craft were linked.
Lucid will return to Earth with two space records. Her mission, expected to last 188 days, is the longest by a woman and a record for an American.
In an interview on Tuesday she said she was looking forward to seeing her family and freshening up.
"I haven't had a shower since March 22nd," she said. "The guys say I don't smell too bad."
